source_text: Δεινόν μοι ἡ ἀχαριστία καταφαίνεται, δεινὸν καὶ πάνδεινον. παθόντα γάρ τι καλῶς, μὴ καὶ ἀμείβεσθαι πειρᾶσθαι, εἰ καὶ μὴ ἄλλως δυνατὸν, εὐχαριστίαις γοῦν ταῖς διὰ λόγων, ἢ ἀνοήτου πάντῃ καὶ ἀναισθήτου τῶν εὐεργεσιῶν, ἢ ἀμνήμονος. ὅτι δὲ καὶ αἴσθησις, καὶ γνῶσις ὧν ἔπαθε καλῶν προσεγένετο, πρῶτον εἰ μὴ καὶ μνήμη διασώζεται εἰς τὸν ἔπειτα χρόνον, εἰ μὴ καὶ ἀναφέροι τινὰ χάριν τῷ ἄρξαντι τῶν ἀγαθῶν, ἀργὸς οὗτος, καὶ ἀχάριστος, καὶ ἀσεβὴς, ἐξαμαρτάνων οὐ συγγνωστὰ οὔτε μεγάλῳ, οὔτε μικρῷ. εἰ μὲν μέγας τις ἐστὶ καὶ μεγαλόνους, οὐκ ἀνὰ στόμα φέρειν σὺν πάσῃ εὐχαριστίᾳ καὶ τιμῇ, τὰς μεγάλας αὐτοῦ εὐεργεσίας. εἰ δὲ μικρὸς, καὶ εὐκαταφρόνητος, οὐκ ἀνυμνεῖν καὶ εὐφημεῖν πάσῃ τῇ αὐτοῦ δυνάμει τὸν, οὐ μεγάλων μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ μικρῶν εὐεργέτην. τοῖς μὲν οὖν μείζοσι καὶ διαβεβηκόσι δυνάμει ψυχῆς, οἷα δὴ ἐκ πλείονος περιουσίας καὶ μεγάλου πλούτου, μείζους καὶ φιλοτιμοτέρας ἀναγκαῖον ἀποδιδόναι τοῖς εὐεργέταις, τὰς κατὰ δύναμιν εὐφημίας. τοῖς δὲ μικροῖς καὶ ἐν στενῷ καθεστῶσιν, οὐδ᾽ αὖθις ἀμελεῖν, οὐδὲ ῥᾳθυμεῖν προσήκει. οὐδ᾽ ἀναπεπτωκέναι, ὡς οὐδὲν ἄξιον φέρειν, οὐδὲ τέλειον δυναμένοις· ἀλλ᾽ οἷα πένητας μὲν, εὐγνώμονας δὲ, οὐ τὴν τοῦ τιμωμένου, τὴν δ᾽ αὐτῶν δύναμιν μετρήσαντας, ἐκ τῆς παρούσης δυνάμεως ἀναφέρειν τὰς τιμὰς, χαριέσσας ἴσως ἐσομένας καὶ καταθυμίους τῷ τιμωμένῳ, καὶ οὐκ ἐν δευτέρᾳ χώρᾳ παρ᾽ αὐτῷ τῶν μεγάλων καὶ πολλῶν, εἰ σύν τινι προθυμίᾳ μείζονι καὶ γνώμῃ προσφέροιεν ὁλοκλήρῳ. οὕτως ἐν ἱεραῖς βίβλοις φέρεται, ὅτι δὴ μικρά τις καὶ πτωχὴ γυνὴ ἅμα πλουσίοις καὶ δυνατοῖς, οἳ προσέφερον ἐκ τοῦ πλούτου μεγάλα καὶ πολυτελῆ, μόνη, μικρὰ μὲν καὶ ἐλάχιστα, πάντα δὲ ὅμως τὰ ὄντα αὐτῇ συμβαλομένη, τὴν τῆς πλείονος δόσεως μαρτυρίαν ἀπηνέγκατο. οὐ γὰρ οἶμαι, τῷ ποσῷ τῆς διδομένης ὕλης οὔσης ἔξωθεν, τῆς δὲ προσφερούσης γνώμης, μᾶλλον καὶ προαιρέσει τὴν φιλοτιμίαν καὶ τὴν μεγαλοπρέπειαν, ὁ ἱερὸς λόγος ἐσταθμήσατο. οὐ τοίνυν οὐδὲ ἡμᾶς ἀποκνεῖν πάντῃ προσῆκεν διὰ τοῦ μὴ ἐξισωθήσεσθαι τὴν εὐχαριστίαν ταῖς εὐεργεσίαις· ἀλλὰ πᾶν τοὐναντίον τολμᾶν καὶ πειρᾶσθαι. εἰ καὶ μὴ τὰς ἴσας, τὰς γοῦν δυνατὰς προσφέρειν, ὡς ἐν ἀμοιβῇ τιμάς. εἴπως τῆς τελείας διαμαρτάνων, τῆς ἐπὶ μέρους γοῦν τεύξηται ἡμῖν ὁ λόγος, τὴν παντελῆ τῆς ἀχαριστίας δόξαν διαδράς.
thought_title: Ingratitude is terrible; even the poor must give what they can
orientation: Ingratitude is a terrible thing, so even one who can give little must offer what thanks he can.
pass_a_gloss: terrible to me ingratitude appears, δεινόν and all-terrible. For having been treated well, not to try to repay — if not otherwise possible, at least with thanks through words — is of one either senseless wholly and insensible of the benefits, or forgetful. But that perception and knowledge of the goods he suffered came to him — first, unless memory also preserves into later time, unless he render some thanks to the one who began the goods, this one is idle, ungrateful, impious, sinning things not pardonable neither for great nor for small. If he is great and great-minded, [unpardonable] not to carry on the mouth with all εὐχαριστία and honor the great εὐεργεσίαι; if small and easily despised, not to hymn and praise with all his power the benefactor not of great only but of small. To the greater and surpassing in power of soul, as from greater abundance and great wealth, it is necessary to render greater and more lavish praises to benefactors, according to power. To the small and those in narrow straits it is not fitting in turn to neglect nor be careless, nor to have fallen back as not able to bring anything worthy or complete; but as poor yet grateful, measuring not the power of the honored but their own, to bring honors from present δύναμις, which will be perhaps pleasing and welcome to the honored, and not in second place with him to the great and many, if with greater eagerness and whole mind they offer. So in sacred books it is recorded that a small and poor woman, with the rich and powerful who offered from their wealth great and costly, alone, small and least, yet all that she had contributing, carried off the testimony of the greater giving. For I think not by the quantity of the given material, being outside, but of the offering intent, rather by choice, did the sacred word weigh the generosity and magnificence. So neither for us is it fitting to shrink back wholly because the εὐχαριστία will not be made equal to the εὐεργεσίαι; but quite the opposite to dare and to try; if not equal, at least possible honors to offer as in return; so that, failing of the complete, our λόγος may at least obtain the partial, escaping the total δόξα of ἀχαριστία.

pass_b_english: Ingratitude seems to me a terrible thing, terrible, indeed utterly terrible. For when someone has been treated well and does not even try to repay it, if in no other way, then at least with thanks spoken in words, he is either wholly senseless and unaware of the kindness done him, or forgetful. And if someone did at first perceive and recognize the good he received, yet memory does not keep it into the time that follows, and he does not render some thanks to the author of those good things, he is idle, ungrateful and impious, and his offense is unpardonable, whether he is great or small. If he is great and great-minded, it is unpardonable not to have his benefactor's great kindnesses on his lips with all thanksgiving and honor. If he is small and of no account, it is unpardonable not to sing the praises, and speak well, with all his strength, of the one who has done him good not only in great things but in small things too.

Those who are greater and stand above others in strength of soul must, as from a larger surplus and great wealth, render to their benefactors greater and more generous praises, as far as their power allows. Yet the small and those in straitened circumstances in their turn ought not to neglect this or grow careless, nor give up, as if they could bring nothing worthy or complete. Like people who are poor but grateful, they should measure not the power of the one honored but their own, and bring their honors out of the power they have. These will perhaps prove pleasing and welcome to the one honored, and with him they will not stand second to great and many gifts, if they are offered with greater eagerness and a whole heart. So it is recorded in the sacred books that a small and poor woman, among the rich and powerful who were offering great and costly gifts from their wealth, contributed small things, the very least, yet all that she had, and she alone carried off the testimony of having given more (Mark 12:41–44; Luke 21:1–4). For I think the sacred word did not weigh generosity and magnificence by the amount of the material given, which is outside a person, but by the intention of the one offering it, or rather by the choice.

So neither ought we to shrink back altogether because our thanksgiving will not equal the benefits. Quite the opposite: we ought to dare and to try, and to offer by way of return, if not equal honors, then at least the honors we can, in the hope that, even if our speech fails to give complete thanks, it may at least give partial thanks, and escape the name of utter ingratitude.
notes: Clear allusion to the poor widow's offering; the wording 'πάντα ... τὰ ὄντα αὐτῇ' answers Mark 12:44 ('all she had') and Luke 21:4, so both Gospel passages are cited. The print's abbreviations near the end are expanded as 'τὴν εὐχαριστίαν ταῖς εὐεργεσίαις' (doubtful expansion of two τ-ligatures); the sense 'our thanksgiving will not equal the benefits' does not depend on the exact case endings. In the second sentence the predicate 'unpardonable' is supplied twice from the preceding 'οὐ συγγνωστά', which governs both infinitive clauses ('not to carry on his lips', 'not to sing the praises'). 'Did at first perceive' keeps πρῶτον with προσεγένετο. 'She alone carried off the testimony' attaches μόνη to ἀπηνέγκατο. 'A whole heart' renders γνώμῃ ὁλοκλήρῳ ('whole mind, entire intent').
